strengths: Soundness: The continuous-template/pixel-averaging model is precisely formulated, and Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give interpretable sufficient conditions connecting resolution, deformation invariance, and class separation. The extensive appendices make much of the argument auditable.

Significance: The constructive CNN analysis usefully relates deformation-covering complexity, filter count, image resolution, and finite-sample error; this is a more informative perspective than a generic dimension-dependent bound.

Originality: Treating within-class randomness as template deformation rather than additive noise provides a useful statistical viewpoint, even though it builds on established pattern-theory, registration, and functional-data ideas.
Presentation: The motivation, notation, figures, and high-level proof structure are generally clear, and the paper distinguishes the inverse-mapping, alignment, and CNN approaches well.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly discusses the optimization gap, background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and complex deformations. The experiments use standard datasets, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The CNN results are not proved at their stated generality. Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 assume only Assumptions 1, 2(i), and 3 and explicitly claim applicability to non-invertible deformations, but Proposition B.4/B.5 assumes that supp(f∘A) lies in [0,1]^2 and uses the change-of-variables identity in Eq. (90). The condition supp(f)⊆A([0,1]^2) does not imply that support property for non-injective A, and the displayed identity also requires injectivity or a multiplicity argument. Added global injectivity/support and norm-preservation assumptions appear necessary.

Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation threshold is not established. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary distance ||f1-f0||/||f0||, whereas the sufficient results use D, an infimum over amplitudes and deformations. Since D can be smaller, no lower bound on D follows. Moreover, the construction is tied to a fixed deformation tuple. Thus the text overstates this theorem as a matching lower bound for Eqs. (12) and (23).

Soundness: The cross-entropy proof equates misclassification with P(sign(kf(X))<0) in Eq. (125), although the classifier's strict >1/2 rule can also err at zero margin. No assumption rules out positive probability of ties. Several other derivations contain repairable inaccuracies, such as the scaling factor for ||f1-f0|| in the proof of Theorem 3.8.

Evidence and significance: Every experimental class is generated by deforming one selected image. This directly enforces the noiseless single-template model and removes genuine within-class variation, so near-zero error is largely a model-recovery sanity check rather than evidence about image classification. Only selected binary pairs are tested, with no standard baselines, natural train/test splits, robustness tests, or uncertainty intervals.

Theory–experiment connection: The implemented CNNs in Table 1 use ordinary 10×10 filters and Adam, while the guarantees concern ideal ERM over a specialized block-structured architecture with 2|A_d^α| filters and prescribed depth. The experiments therefore do not test the theorem's architecture, separation rate, covering-number dependence, or optimization assumptions.

Reproducibility: There is no code or complete configuration. The deformation ranges, selected template identities, grayscale/background-removal procedure, epochs, batch size, stopping rule, seeds, and several architectural details are omitted. Test sets of only 50 or 200 examples and medians over ten runs are inadequate for resolving the small reported errors.

Reach and presentation: Exact zero background, full visibility, one template per class, no observation noise, known deformation family, and deterministic labels make the setting highly restrictive. The manuscript acknowledges several of these limitations but still makes broad claims about CNN image classification. At 30 pages before proofs and 81 pages total, it is also substantially too long and diffuse for an ICML main-track presentation. Overall, the mathematical viewpoint has merit, but the proof-scope gaps and weak empirical validation require substantial revision before acceptance.

strengths: Originality and significance: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-5w5fcwt3/call-04be9fdef5c04997966b2a9c1d79c7b9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} develops a useful statistical perspective in which image variability arises from deformations of class templates rather than independent pixel noise. Although template/deformation models are classical, connecting resolution-dependent identifiability, alignment classifiers, and CNN generalization is meaningfully original.

Soundness—positive aspects: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give explicit sufficient conditions for perfect classification, while the pixel-aliasing construction in Theorem 3.8 captures a genuine resolution barrier. The appendices provide extensive proof details rather than treating the main results as black boxes.

The CNN construction is conceptually informative: template-deformation filters, global max pooling, and a finite deformation cover yield an explicit representability result (Theorem 4.2), followed by VC-based bounds for both 0–1 and cross-entropy ERM (Theorems 4.1 and 4.4). This offers more insight than a generic capacity bound alone.

Presentation is generally structured and mathematically readable, with helpful figures and a broad discussion connecting the work to functional-data registration, pattern theory, scattering transforms, and equivariant networks.

The authors appropriately acknowledge important limitations, including idealized ERM optimization, noise, occlusion, multiple objects, structured backgrounds, and sharp edges. The work uses established benchmark datasets and raises no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central CNN guarantees are not established under their stated assumptions. Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 assume only Assumption 2(i), and the paper explicitly claims that invertibility is unnecessary. Nevertheless, Proposition B.4 and the proof of Proposition B.5 repeatedly infer that supp(f∘A) is contained in [0,1]^2 and Equation (90) uses a change-of-variables equality. These steps do not follow for a general non-injective map satisfying 2(i). An area-formula argument might repair one inequality, but the support and zero-padding arguments still require an injectivity/proper-preimage or explicit boundary condition. Thus the advertised non-invertible generality needs either a new proof or materially stronger assumptions.

Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d deformation-aware separation is not proved by Theorem 3.8. That theorem bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between f0 and f1, whereas the sufficient results use D from Equations (12), (23), or (32), which minimizes over amplitudes and deformations. No lower bound on D is established, nor is the constructed distance localized from above as order 1/d. Consequently, statements that Theorem 3.8 proves necessity or matching optimality for D overstate the result.

A further technical gap occurs in Lemma 3.5: λ ranges over the unbounded set |λ|≥Clower, yet the proof claims a finite order-d² cover by discretizing λ at absolute resolution order 1/d. The result may be recoverable by discretizing 1/λ, but the supplied construction does not prove it.

Significance is constrained by the model: each class has one deterministic template, images are noiseless, backgrounds are exactly zero, objects are fully visible, and the deformation family is known. These assumptions largely eliminate the intra-class semantic variation that makes real image classification difficult. Section 7 discusses extensions honestly, but does not establish them.

The empirical evidence is too weak to support the stated corroboration. Sections 5.1–5.2 select one image per class and classify only synthetic transformations of those same images; this is template matching rather than classification on MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet populations. There are no standard, equivariant, scattering, or registration baselines; resolution and separation are not varied; theoretical rates are not tested; and only medians over 10 runs with small test sets are shown without uncertainty.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code is provided, and the paper omits template indices, random seeds, deformation distributions and parameter ranges, exact preprocessing/segmentation, training epochs, batch size, detailed dense architecture, and inverse-cover implementation. Table 1 and the Adam learning rate are insufficient to reproduce Figures 9–11.

Presentation requires substantial revision for an ICML main-track submission: the main body is approximately 30 single-column pages before 45 pages of proofs, is repetitive, and is not in anonymous ICML format. Several interpretations—especially the lower-bound optimality and the claim that the experiments validate Assumption 3—should be weakened or justified. Overall, the ideas and technical effort are clear merits, but the theorem-assumption mismatch and evidential/reproducibility deficiencies currently outweigh them.

The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

strengths: Originality/significance: The deformation-orbit formulation offers a useful alternative to treating pixels as unrelated covariates. It connects image registration, functional data analysis, and CNN invariance while highlighting how increasing resolution can help rather than cause a dimensionality curse.

Soundness: The constructive upper bounds are substantial. Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 analyze alignment-based classifiers, while Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 combine an explicit filter construction with VC/entropy arguments to obtain sample-dependent CNN error bounds.
The manuscript treats several deformation families, gives covering-number calculations, and makes the role of resolution, deformation complexity, and network size relatively explicit.
Presentation is generally clear and visually polished despite the technical length. The extensive appendix makes most derivations traceable.

The discussion honestly acknowledges zero-background assumptions, noise, occlusion, sharp edges, and the gap between ERM theory and gradient-based training. The work raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary template distance ||f1−f0||₂/||f0||₂, whereas the upper results use the orbit distance D, an infimum over brightness, shifts, and scalings. No corresponding lower bound on D is proved. Moreover, the theorem states templates that work for every sufficiently large d, but its proof constructs f1 using a d-dependent perturbation g.

Soundness: The CNN theorems assume only Assumption 2(i) and explicitly advertise applicability to non-invertible deformations. However, Propositions B.4–B.5 use that supp(f∘A) lies inside [0,1]². The condition supp(f)⊆A([0,1]²) does not imply this preimage-support property without injectivity. An additional full-support or invertibility assumption is needed, so the CNN guarantees are not proved for the stated deformation class.

Significance is limited by the highly idealized model: each class has one fixed template, variation is exclusively a known family of label-independent deformations and brightness changes, objects are fully visible, and images have nonnegative signals with exactly zero background. These exclude much of the semantic and within-class variability of real image classification.

The experiments use only one selected image per class and synthetically deform it for both training and testing. They therefore verify an in-model orbit-matching task, not classification on naturally varying MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet data. They do not test the predicted dependence on resolution, separation D, covering size, or the stated rates, and report medians without uncertainty.

The experimental 10×10 Keras CNNs trained with Adam do not closely instantiate the constructive block-filter/deep-max architecture or exact ERM analyzed theoretically. Consequently, the numerical results provide little evidence for the CNN theorems or their optimization relevance.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code is provided, and the manuscript omits exact template identifiers, deformation distributions and ranges, random seeds, epochs, batch size, stopping rules, and complete pooling/head specifications.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper develops a distinctive statistical perspective in which within-class image variability arises from transformations of functional templates rather than additive noise. It treats translations, scaling, brightness, rotations, affine maps, and nonlinear warps in one framework. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8_wy5k66/call-f7e3114a5f4544d89f3b3bf8c03f8816/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Soundness: The upper-bound theory is technically substantial and largely self-contained. Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give explicit resolution-dependent conditions for perfect inverse-mapping and alignment classification, while Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 connect CNN approximation, deformation-class covering complexity, network capacity, and finite-sample error. Extensive appendices expose the constructions and proof details.

Presentation: The manuscript motivates the functional-data viewpoint clearly, defines its assumptions and separation quantities explicitly, and uses helpful illustrations to connect alignment, convolution, and invariance. The discussion appropriately acknowledges ERM optimization, background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and richer transformations as limitations or future directions.

The experiments provide useful qualitative sanity checks across MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet templates: alignment succeeds on the intended synthetic model, inverse mapping improves with finer discretization, and CNN error generally falls with sample size and capacity.

Reproducibility and ethics: The mathematical contribution is reproducible from the detailed definitions and proofs. The work uses standard public image benchmarks and presents no material human-subject, privacy, or deployment-related ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness/scope: The central model assumes one fixed template per class, exact deformation-only variation, nonnegative Lipschitz images, full object visibility, and effectively zero background. Consequently, the zero Bayes error and one-example-per-class results exclude most natural intra-class variation, sensor noise, clutter, and occlusion. Claims about image classification broadly should therefore be qualified more sharply.

The advertised optimality of the 1/d separation condition is not established in the paper's own deformation-invariant metric. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary distance between f0 and f1, whereas the upper results use D, an infimum over intensity changes and transformations; a lower bound on ordinary distance does not lower-bound D. Its proof also writes the coordinate-rescaling factor as ξξ′ instead of sqrt(ξξ′) for an L2 norm. The order-level conclusion may be repairable, but the claimed matching lower bound is unresolved as written.

The empirical evidence is much weaker than the theory: every task is generated by repeatedly augmenting only one selected template per class, and testing uses the identical synthetic deformation mechanism. Thus the experiments mainly verify an easy realizable setting and do not show robustness to genuine within-class diversity or model misspecification.

There is a substantial theory–experiment gap. The proofs construct template-dependent, block-structured filters and a particular depth/width scaling tied to the covering set, whereas the experiments use generic 10x10 filters and do not test predicted dependence on resolution, separation, or covering complexity. No conventional CNN, raw nearest-neighbor, registration, invariant-network, or scattering baseline is included, and only medians over 10 repetitions with small test sets are reported without uncertainty.

Experimental reproducibility is inadequate: no code is provided, and the manuscript omits deformation ranges, exact template identities, preprocessing/segmentation details, training epochs, batch size, initialization seeds, stopping criteria, and the precise number of fully connected layers. Table 1 and the Adam learning rate are insufficient to reconstruct the experiments.

strengths: Originality/significance: The deformation-centric statistical formulation offers a useful alternative to treating pixels as unrelated covariates. Its separation quantities and resolution-dependent analysis provide potentially valuable insight into invariance and image classification.

Soundness: The paper develops substantial theory, including guarantees for inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers and CNN expressivity/generalization results. Most arguments are supported by detailed auxiliary lemmas covering discretization, normalization, approximation error, and VC complexity.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and self-contained, with helpful figures illustrating alignment, deformation orbits, and the matched-filter CNN construction. Connections to registration, functional data analysis, scattering transforms, and equivariant networks are discussed.

Limitations/ethics: The authors candidly identify important unresolved settings such as background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and optimization. The theoretical and synthetic nature of the work presents no obvious material ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The CNN results are not valid at their advertised generality. Section 4 says invertibility is unnecessary, but Proposition B.4, Eq. (90), and Proposition B.5 use change of variables and infer that supp(f composed with A) is contained in the image domain. Assumption 2(i) does not justify these steps for general non-injective Lipschitz deformations. Theorems 4.1-4.2 require stronger injectivity, support, or multiplicity assumptions, or a revised proof.

The claimed necessity of the 1/d separation criterion is not established. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the direct distance between pixel-indistinguishable templates, whereas the operative quantity D is an infimum over brightness, shifts, scalings, and deformation compositions. No corresponding lower bound on D for the constructed templates is proved.

The experiments do not convincingly support the central claims. Every class is produced by deforming a single selected template, so the data instantiate the assumed model almost exactly. Moreover, the trained Keras CNNs are not the theorem's deformation-cover construction or globally optimized ERMs; the experiments do not test the predicted dependence on separation, covering number, resolution, or the V/n rate.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper provides no code, template identifiers, augmentation ranges or distributions, random seeds, epoch counts, batch sizes, stopping rules, detailed preprocessing, or exact inverse-cover construction. Results use only 50 or 200 test examples and report medians over ten repetitions without uncertainty estimates.

Significance is sharply limited by the noiseless one-template-per-class setting, exactly zero backgrounds, fully visible single objects, nonnegative grayscale inputs, known deformation family, and strong orbit separation. Real datasets serve only as seeds for synthetic transformations, so applicability to natural within-class variation or commonly trained CNNs remains unsubstantiated.

Several repairable technical and presentation issues further reduce confidence: Assumption 3 is not rigorously verified for the showcased deformation families; Lemma 3.5's proof uses an absolute grid for an unbounded wavelength parameter; the cross-entropy proof mishandles threshold ties through sgn(kf)<0; and Eq. (37) has inconsistent test-set indexing. A careful proof audit and much stronger evaluation are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Originality/significance: The functional random-deformation model offers a useful alternative to treating pixels as unrelated covariates, and explicitly connects image resolution, class separation, and deformation-class complexity.

Soundness: For the noiseless invertible setting, the alignment and inverse-mapping analyses are coherent, and the paper provides detailed proofs. The matched-filter CNN construction and its VC-based bounds cover both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.
Presentation: The manuscript is logically organized, defines its model and separation quantities carefully, and uses helpful figures to explain alignment, filtering, and the lower-bound construction.

Limitations/ethics: The authors candidly acknowledge computational infeasibility of inverse mapping, sensitivity to backgrounds and multiple objects, missing optimization guarantees, and difficulties with occlusion and sharp edges. No material ethical concern is apparent for this primarily theoretical work using standard non-human image datasets.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the unaligned distance ||f1-f0||2/||f0||2, whereas the sufficient conditions use D, an infimum over brightness changes and deformations. A lower bound on the former does not imply D=Omega(1/d); the constructed alternative also depends on fixed deformation parameters. Thus the stated necessity of the separation conditions in Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 remains unsupported.

Soundness: The CNN theorems explicitly claim not to require invertible deformations, but Proposition B.4 and Proposition B.5 repeatedly assume that supp(f composed with A) is contained in [0,1]^2 and use change-of-variables/support identities. Assumption 2(i), namely that the template-support rectangle is contained in A([0,1]^2), does not imply this support containment for a non-injective A. The results need an additional proper-support condition, a careful area-formula argument, or restriction to invertible maps.

Significance: The model assumes every example in a class is an exact deformation of one fixed template, with full visibility and essentially no background or observation noise. Consequently, the striking one-example-per-class guarantee largely follows from an unusually strong orbit model and does not address ordinary within-class morphological or semantic variation.

Evidence: The experiments generate both training and test data by augmenting the same single exemplar per class, making them close to a direct verification of the assumed model. They do not test natural within-class data, the predicted dependence on d, D, or covering cardinality, or the theoretical CNN architecture. The claim that wider experimental CNNs implement a finer deformation cover is not demonstrated.

Reproducibility: The augmentation ranges and distributions, selected image identifiers, preprocessing details, inverse-map grids, number of epochs, batch size, initialization, stopping rule, and random seeds are absent, and no code is provided. Test sets of only 50 or 200 examples with medians over ten runs and no dispersion estimates are inadequate support for claims of zero error or convergence rates.

Presentation/claims: The manuscript sometimes overstates what follows from the analysis, including that the simulations corroborate the theoretical rates, that V/n is minimax-optimal for this generative model, and that CNN robustness to independent background noise follows heuristically from the CLT. These should be narrowed or supported by additional results.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-n83by6av/call-529542c660474daf9440888a5aabf746/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} defines a precise continuous-template deformation model, explicitly accounts for pixel averaging, and states assumptions and separation conditions clearly.

Technical contribution: The inverse-mapping and alignment analyses, followed by CNN expressivity and ERM bounds for both 0-1 and cross-entropy losses, form a substantial and largely self-contained theoretical development.

Significance and originality: Treating additional pixels as improved resolution rather than additional unrelated covariates is an insightful perspective. Connecting functional-data alignment, deformation orbits, and CNN invariance could stimulate useful theory.

Presentation: The paper is organized coherently and supplies extensive proofs, architecture definitions, parameter counts, and illustrative figures. It also acknowledges optimization, noise, occlusion, and multi-object extensions as unresolved.
Ethics: The experiments use established image benchmarks and present no evident material safety or human-subject concern.
weaknesses: Soundness and scope: Every class has exactly one fixed template, labels are deterministic, and all variation is generated by a known deformation family. Central results additionally require noiseless backgrounds, fully visible objects, global regularity, covering, and strong orbit-separation assumptions. Perfect classification with one example per class is consequently a realizability result and does not substantiate broad claims about ordinary image classification.

The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation condition is not established for the paper's deformation-invariant distance D. Theorem 3.8 constructs indistinguishable templates whose raw normalized L2 distance is at least order 1/d, but D is an infimum over rescalings, shifts, and deformations and can only be smaller; no matching lower bound on D is proved.

There are proof gaps needing repair. Equation (90) invokes a change-of-variables equality under Assumption 2(i), although that assumption does not ensure injectivity or a Jacobian lower bound, while the text explicitly claims the CNN result permits noninvertible deformations. An area-formula argument might recover the needed inequality, but it is absent. The cross-entropy proof also equates misclassification with a strict negative-margin event and therefore mishandles exact ties.

The image-alignment guarantee is not uniformly the advertised one-sample-per-class result: its condition contains the sample-dependent maximum scaling factor Xi_n, while Assumption 2' gives no upper bound on scaling. The requirement can worsen with sample size for unbounded deformation distributions.

Evidence and significance: Train and test images are merely augmentations of one selected image per class. There is no evaluation on genuine within-class variability, no meaningful baseline, no uncertainty intervals, and no controlled study varying resolution d, separation D, or deformation complexity. Thus the experiments do not convincingly test the central rates or real-world relevance.

The empirical CNNs do not instantiate the theorem's deformation-cover/matched-filter construction, and Adam is not shown to find the analyzed ERM. The explanation that larger empirical networks provide a finer approximation of the deformation set is therefore unsupported by the reported measurements.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the experiments: deformation ranges and distributions, template identifiers, preprocessing details, epochs or stopping rules, batch sizes, random seeds, and code are not provided. Reporting medians over only ten repetitions with test sets of 50 or 200 images is also fragile.

Originality is narrower than the framing suggests: template deformation, registration, invariant representations, and group-aware CNNs are established ideas; the CNN result combines an oracle bank of template-dependent matched filters with standard VC/entropy generalization machinery. The discussion also misleadingly characterizes uniform neural-network generalization bounds as applying only to non-data-dependent predictors.

Presentation and limitations: The supplied PDF is 81 pages with roughly 29 pages before the appendix, contains author identities and arXiv metadata, and is not compliant with a conventional anonymous ICML main-track submission. Although several extensions are discussed, the paper does not foreground the decisive single-template synthetic-data limitation or discuss benchmark licensing and broader-impact considerations.

Soundness: For the narrow model of noiseless, fully visible deformations of one template per class, the inverse-mapping and alignment analyses are detailed. Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give explicit separation conditions, and Theorem 3.8 provides an informative pixelization-based indistinguishability construction.

The CNN section contains a nontrivial matched-filter expressivity construction and derives explicit ERM bounds through deformation covering numbers and VC complexity for both 0-1 and cross-entropy losses.

Presentation: The motivating distinction between additive noise and geometric variation is clear, and the figures help explain alignment, convolution, pooling, and the lower-bound construction. Connections to registration, functional data analysis, scattering, and equivariant networks are discussed.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly discuss optimization, background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, sharp edges, and perspective transformations. The work uses standard public vision datasets and presents no evident material ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central model assumes every class is generated from exactly one fixed template using only geometric transformations and brightness changes, with no observation noise and fully visible objects. This excludes ordinary intra-class variation such as handwriting style, pose/articulation, texture, and background. Consequently, the broad image-classification motivation is not supported by the proved model.

There is a material assumption gap in the CNN theory. The text claims Theorems 4.1–4.4 accommodate non-invertible deformations, but Propositions B.4–B.5 use both supp(f∘A)⊆[0,1]^2 and the change-of-variables equality in Eq. (90). Neither follows from Assumption 2(i) for a non-injective map. Since Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 rely on Theorem 4.2 and Proposition B.5, the advertised non-invertible scope is unsupported without additional global support, multiplicity, or invertibility assumptions.

The claimed optimality is stronger than the established lower bound: Theorem 3.8 constructs one pixel vector compatible with two templates at selected deformation parameters, but no minimax risk or distributional lower bound is stated for the random model with a specified Q_A. Separately, Lemma 3.5 claims a finite order-d² cover while its proof discretizes the unbounded wavelength λ directly at absolute order 1/d; that argument does not produce a finite cover as written.

Significance/evidence: Every experiment chooses one image per class and generates both training and test sets by applying the assumed transformations to those same templates. The resulting near-zero errors mainly confirm performance on the exact generator; they do not test full MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet class distributions, model misspecification, background noise, or unseen templates.

The empirical CNNs are not tied convincingly to the theoretical architecture: the experiments use fixed 10×10 filters and three heuristic widths, whereas the proofs require block-structured template/deformation filters, global max pooling, a specified depth, and widths determined by |A_d^α|. Assumption 3 and its asserted covering cardinalities are not rigorously verified for the showcased deformation families.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code is provided, and the deformation ranges/distributions, chosen image identifiers, preprocessing details, seeds, epoch counts, batch sizes, initialization, stopping rule, and several architectural details are omitted. Only medians over 10 runs with test sizes 50 or 200 are reported, without dispersion. Equation (37) also inconsistently defines N test examples while referring to samples X_{n+1},…,X_N and summing through X_{n+N}.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: canonicalization/alignment, template matching over transformation orbits, global-pooling invariance, and generic realizable-case VC bounds are established ideas. The pixel-resolution separation analysis is the clearest novel element, but its practical reach remains narrow.

Presentation/compliance: As supplied, the paper has a 30-page main body and 81 pages total, exposes author identities, includes acknowledgments, and bears an arXiv identifier. It is therefore not in anonymous ICML main-track submission form. More importantly for the scientific recommendation, the length does not compensate for the missing real-distribution evaluation and incomplete reproducibility. These evidential and technical issues require substantial revision and prevent acceptance in the present form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-09yyisoy/call-06da4950fa344706b13457099098f243/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} offers an interesting statistical perspective in which pixel count improves resolution rather than merely increasing dimension, connecting deformation models, registration, functional data analysis, and invariant classification.

Soundness: The upper-bound analysis is technically substantial. The assumptions and deformation-aware separation quantities are explicit, and Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give interpretable resolution-dependent guarantees for the inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers.

The constructive CNN analysis is a valuable element: template-matched filters indexed by a deformation cover are combined with VC-dimension and entropy arguments to obtain explicit dependence on n, d, and the cover size for both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.
Presentation: The paper is largely self-contained, illustrates affine and nonlinear deformation classes, and supplies extensive proofs and useful diagrams.

The authors candidly discuss important limitations, including background noise, multiple or occluded objects, sharp edges, perspective transformations, and the gap between ideal ERM and gradient-based optimization. The theoretical and synthetic nature of the work raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established for the paper's actual separation quantity. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between a constructed pair, but D in (12)/(23) is an infimum over intensity and geometric transformations, so that ordinary-distance bound does not imply D is at least order 1/d. Nor is there an n-sample minimax argument with fixed templates under nondegenerate random transformations. This weakens a central necessity claim.

The CNN results are stated as allowing non-invertible deformations, but their proofs repeatedly use that supp(f composed with A) lies in [0,1]^2 and invoke change-of-variables reasoning around (90). Assumption 2(i) does not ensure these properties for a non-injective A. The additional norm-preservation condition mentioned in prose is absent from the theorem statements and does not by itself resolve the support issue.

The experiments do not evaluate natural image classification: each binary task uses only one selected image per class and generates every training and test example by synthetically deforming that same template. Thus the results test an almost exactly specified toy model and provide little evidence for classes with genuine within-class shape, texture, or background variation.

There is a substantial theory-to-experiment mismatch. The guarantees concern globally optimized ERM over a specially constrained CNN with deformation-cover/template filters and prescribed depth, whereas the experiments use 10x10 filters, unspecified fully connected depth, and Adam. Consequently, the numerical trends do not validate the stated CNN rates or construction.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript provides no code and omits deformation ranges, selected image identifiers, detailed preprocessing, complete architectures, epochs, batch sizes, initialization, stopping rules, and random seeds.

The empirical estimates are weak: only 50 or 200 test samples and ten repetitions are used, medians are reported without uncertainty, and sampled zero error is treated as convergence to zero. No experiment varies resolution or measures the separation quantity, despite these being central theoretical variables, and there are no relevant baselines.

Significance is limited by the single-template, noiseless, exact-zero-background, fully visible object model. Several broader claims—such as insight into practical CNN success, overparameterization, and data augmentation—are not directly supported. The unusually long and repetitive presentation further obscures the core contribution.

Soundness: The inverse-mapping and alignment upper bounds are stated under explicit assumptions and supported by extensive proofs. The CNN analysis combines a constructive expressivity result with VC-dimension and entropy arguments for both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.
Presentation: The mathematical setup, deformation examples, and theorem dependencies are mostly clear. The appendix is unusually detailed and makes much of the theoretical analysis auditable.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly acknowledges computationally infeasible alignment, the gap between ERM and gradient-based training, and missing treatment of noise, occlusion, and structured backgrounds. The synthetic experiments present no substantial ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 3.8 does not establish the advertised matching lower bound for the actual orbit distances in (12) or (23). It lower-bounds only the undeformed distance between the constructed templates, whereas D is an infimum over brightness, shifts, scales, and deformations; a lower bound on the former does not imply D is of order 1/d. The central optimality claim therefore remains unsupported.

The CNN results contain repairable but nontrivial proof issues. Equation (90) invokes a change-of-variables equality although Assumption 2(i) does not require injectivity, and (125)-(128) do not correctly handle zero-margin ties under the strict greater-than-1/2 decision rule.

Significance is limited by the noiseless single-template-per-class model. All within-class variability must be a label-independent deformation with multiplicative brightness, full visibility, and essentially zero background. Under separation, the label is deterministic and one sample per class suffices, which is far removed from ordinary image classification with morphology, clutter, texture, and annotation uncertainty.

The CNN guarantee is for global ERM over a specialized architecture whose constructive filters depend on deformed templates and may span the full image. It neither analyzes optimization nor matches the experimental 10-by-10-filter Adam networks. The claimed V/n minimax optimality is generic VC theory, not a lower bound for this deformation model.

The empirical evidence is not convincing: each task uses one selected source image per class and generates both training and test sets solely by deforming those same two images. There is no evaluation on unseen templates, no standard or invariant-learning baselines, no verification of the separation and covering assumptions, and only medians over 10 trials with test sets of 50 or 200 examples.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper omits source-image identifiers, augmentation ranges and distributions, interpolation/fill settings, CNN depth, epochs, batch size, initialization, stopping criteria, seeds, uncertainty estimates, and a code repository. Consequently, even the synthetic experiments cannot be reliably reconstructed.

Presentation is much too long for the ICML main-track format as supplied: 30 pages precede the appendix and the PDF totals 81 pages. It is also a named arXiv version rather than an anonymized conference manuscript, and several practical claims—especially robustness to background noise and the interpretation of larger CNNs as finer deformation covers—are asserted without evidence.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript develops a precise functional deformation model and explicit separation measures. Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give constructive exact-classification guarantees at order-1/d separation, supported by substantial proofs. Reviewed manuscript: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-negvbxxi/call-9f44e5c112bb49b18c25bfbc82b002fa/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Originality and significance: Viewing higher resolution as a more accurate observation of a deformed bivariate template, rather than as additional unrelated covariates, is insightful. Connecting registration, orbit separation, and statistical image-classification rates offers useful new understanding.

Soundness: The CNN analysis is ambitious and unusually explicit. It constructs deformation-indexed matched filters with global max pooling and derives bounds for both 0-1 and clipped cross-entropy ERM, exposing dependence on resolution, deformation-cover complexity, and network size.

Presentation: The model, classifiers, and principal theorems are generally explained clearly, while the figures make the alignment and matched-filter intuitions accessible. The extensive appendix facilitates technical inspection.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly discusses the ERM-versus-optimization gap, background noise, multiple objects, occlusion, sharp edges, and perspective transformations. Its use of standard vision benchmarks with synthetic transformations presents no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness (decisive): The CNN theorems assume only Assumption 2(i) and explicitly claim that invertibility is unnecessary, but Appendix B uses consequences not implied by that assumption. In particular, Lemma B.3(iv) is applied as though supp(f composed with A) is contained in [0,1]^2, Proposition B.4 asserts this containment, and Equation (90) uses an injective-style change of variables. The condition that the template-support rectangle is contained in A([0,1]^2) does not ensure these properties for a non-injective A. Consequently, Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 are not established for their stated deformation class; an injectivity/no-cropping condition or a revised proof is needed.

Soundness: Theorem 3.8 has a quantifier mismatch. It states that fixed templates exist which produce identical pixels for every sufficiently large d, whereas its proof constructs the perturbation g from d-dependent pixel tents S_jl. A fixed continuous nonzero difference cannot have zero integral on every cell of arbitrarily fine grids. The likely intended per-d minimax construction is repairable, but the claimed matching necessity result is false as written.

Significance: The model places all within-class variation in known geometric deformations of one deterministic template and excludes observation noise, nonzero backgrounds, cropping, and genuine shape or texture variation. Under separation, the label is therefore deterministic. The striking one-example-per-class and zero-error conclusions have limited bearing on ordinary image classification; Section 7 proposes relevant extensions but does not analyze them.

Soundness and practical relevance: The realizability filters depend on the unknown templates and a deformation cover, while learning assumes a global ERM, including under the intractable 0-1 loss. The acknowledged optimization gap is substantial: the Adam-trained 10x10-filter networks in the experiments are not the constructed architecture, so their success does not validate the theoretical learning mechanism or bounds.

Evaluation: Each task uses only one selected image per class as a template and generates both training and test sets through the same augmentation mechanism. This is an especially favorable synthetic test of the assumed model, not an evaluation on real within-class distributions. There are no standard 1-NN, registration, scattering, group-equivariant, or augmentation baselines; no controlled tests over d, separation, or covering complexity; and only medians from 10 repetitions with N=50 or 200 test samples and no uncertainty estimates. Thus the claim that the experiments corroborate the theory is too strong.

Reproducibility and presentation: The manuscript does not provide code, deformation distributions or ranges, exemplar identifiers/ImageNet synsets, complete preprocessing and segmentation details, normalization confirmation, training epochs, batch sizes, stopping rules, seeds, or the exact inverse-grid implementation. Figures 9 and 11 cannot be reliably reproduced. The 30-page main narrative is also much too diffuse for an ICML paper, and the novelty relative to classical registration/orbit and invariant-representation methods could be distilled more sharply. These issues, together with the theorem-scope problems, outweigh the paper's clear conceptual merits in its current form.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript defines a precise deformation-based generative model and derives explicit sufficient conditions linking class separation, pixel resolution, and exact classification (Theorems 3.1 and 3.7), supported by extensive appendices.

Originality: Treating pixels as discretizations of deformed template functions provides a useful alternative to generic high-dimensional classification and yields an interesting explanation of when increasing resolution can help.

Technical contribution: The constructive CNN approximation result and its combination with VC-dimension and covering-number arguments produce explicit dependencies on sample size, resolution, and deformation-class complexity for both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.
Presentation: The main constructions are motivated clearly, and the alignment and filter illustrations make the intuition accessible despite the manuscript's length.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly acknowledge computational infeasibility, the ERM-versus-optimization gap, background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and perspective effects. The experiments use public datasets with synthetic transformations, and no material ethical risk is apparent in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-twqnpjsh/call-2aab573370144cd3a332cdebce201b9e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Significance: The central model assumes exactly one noiseless template per class, exact zero background, full visibility, smooth nonnegative templates, and all within-class variability arising from a known deformation family and brightness. These assumptions make the label deterministic and permit perfect classification from one example per class, but exclude most difficulty in natural image classification; several broad claims about real image variability and CNN performance therefore exceed the established scope.

Soundness: The claimed matching lower bound is incomplete. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the unwarped L2 distance between constructed templates, whereas the sufficient conditions use D, an infimum over amplitudes, shifts, and deformations. No lower bound on D is proved, so the assertion that the D proportional to 1/d criterion is optimal does not follow as written.

Soundness: Section 4 says invertibility is unnecessary, but Proposition B.4 infers support and boundary properties of f composed with A that do not follow from Assumption 2(i) for non-injective A, while equation (90) is written as a one-to-one change-of-variables identity. The cross-entropy proof also equates threshold error with a strict-sign event in equation (125), omitting possible zero-logit ties. These gaps appear potentially repairable but affect central guarantees.

Theory-practice connection: The CNN results concern existence and global ERM over a specially structured, bounded-weight architecture. The experiments instead train 10-by-10-filter networks with Adam, and their correspondence to the block-filter architecture, covering set, and global optimizer used by the theory is not established.

Evaluation: Every class is generated by deforming one selected template image. Thus the experiments reproduce the assumed two-orbit problem rather than testing natural within-class variation. They provide no standard baselines, real-dataset train/test experiment, resolution or separation sweep, deformation-complexity ablation, rate fit, or uncertainty beyond medians over 10 runs with only 50 or 200 test examples.

Reproducibility: There is no code, template-image identifier, transformation distribution or parameter range, seed, epoch count, batch size, stopping rule, full layer specification, or sufficiently precise inverse-mapping implementation. The numerical results cannot be independently reproduced from the manuscript.

Originality and presentation: Template-orbit classification, registration, and invariant representations are classical; the new value lies mainly in the particular bounds, but comparison with learned alignment and modern equivariant/invariant methods is limited. As supplied, the paper is also an author-identified 81-page arXiv manuscript with roughly 30 pages before the proof appendix, rather than an anonymized, concise ICML submission.

strengths: Originality/significance: The continuous-template deformation model offers a useful alternative to treating pixels as unrelated covariates and captures the important insight that increasing resolution can simplify, rather than worsen, classification.

Soundness: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give explicit, interpretable guarantees for inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers, with detailed assumptions and proofs connecting pixelization error to an O(1/d) separation scale.
The constructive CNN analysis is ambitious: it relates deformation-cover complexity, resolution, architecture size, and sample size, and treats both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.

Presentation: The manuscript is largely self-contained and makes helpful connections to functional data analysis, image registration, scattering transforms, and invariant CNNs. The diagrams clarify the alignment and max-pooling constructions.

Limitations/ethics: The discussion candidly identifies background noise, occlusion, sharp edges, perspective effects, and the gap between exact ERM and gradient training. The standard benchmark-image experiments raise no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation criterion is not established in the paper's own deformation-invariant metric. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds only the untransformed distance ||f1-f0||2/||f0||2, whereas D in (23) additionally infimizes over brightness, scaling, and translation. A lower bound on the former does not imply D is Ω(1/d). Moreover, the constructed f1 depends on fixed deformation parameters, so the discussion of random deformations requires qualification.

Soundness: The central CNN proof uses properties not supplied by its assumptions. Equation (90) asserts a one-to-one change-of-variables equality under Assumption 2(i), although that assumption does not require injectivity; Proposition B.4 likewise infers supp(f∘A)⊆[0,1]^2 and f(A(0,0))=0, which need not hold for a non-injective A. These steps feed Proposition B.5 and hence Theorems 4.2, 4.1, and 4.4. An area-formula argument or stronger assumptions might repair the result, but that argument is absent.

The cross-entropy proof has an additional logical gap: equation (125) equates the classifier using p2>1/2 with an event using a strict negative signed margin. A zero margin misclassifies a class-1 example under the stated tie rule but is excluded from that event; no zero-tie probability assumption is provided.

Significance: The model assumes one noiseless template per class, zero background, full visibility, nonnegative images, and within-class variability consisting only of a known deformation family. The experiments generate both training and test data from exactly one selected template per label, so near-perfect classification does not demonstrate robustness to genuine intra-class variation.

The theoretical CNN is an oracle-style construction with filters derived from the unknown deformed templates, global ERM, and potentially very large deformation covers. Table 1 instead studies ordinary 10×10-filter CNNs trained by Adam. The experiments therefore do not directly validate the proposed architecture, approximation theorem, separation condition, or predicted rate.

Reproducibility is inadequate: Section 5 omits the deformation parameter ranges and distributions, chosen template identifiers, several preprocessing details, epochs, batch size, initialization and stopping rules, precise inverse-map grids, and code. Figures 9 and 11 report only medians over 10 repetitions with test sets of 50 or 200 and provide no dispersion estimates.

The evaluation lacks ordinary nearest-neighbor, registration, equivariant-CNN, or scattering baselines and does not vary resolution, separation, noise, or deformation-cover size in a way that tests the central theoretical dependencies. Thus the empirical evidence is substantially weaker than the manuscript's claim that it corroborates the theory.

Presentation is generally clear but overly long, and several notation or prose errors obscure important points, including ambiguous support-index definitions, inconsistent norm scaling in the proof of Theorem 3.8, and the unsupported explanation that more training samples make the fixed inverse-mapping discretization denser.

strengths: Soundness: The paper states an explicit deformation-based generative model and derives concrete links among image resolution, orbit separation, deformation-covering complexity, network size, and sample complexity. The extensive appendix makes most constructions traceable.

Originality and significance: The deformation-invariant separation quantities and the analysis of a shallow CNN with global max pooling provide a potentially useful theoretical benchmark connecting pattern theory, functional-data registration, and statistical learning.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally organized clearly, with helpful illustrations and theorem-level statements that distinguish inverse mapping, alignment, and CNN approaches. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-h1hdr7l2/call-1424396d79bc40e99da8bd7fb3b0e2e6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Limitations and ethics: Section 7 openly acknowledges background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, sharp edges, and the gap between ERM and practical optimization. The largely theoretical and synthetic study raises no major unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness and scope: Every class is represented by one fixed template, and all within-class variability is restricted to label-independent geometric deformation and brightness. Objects are fully visible, backgrounds are exactly zero, and observations contain no noise. Under orbit separation the label is deterministic, so perfect one-example classification and realizable-case VC rates are much less informative than the manuscript's broader claims about practical image classification.

The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established for the paper's actual separation metric. Theorem 3.8 constructs pixel-indistinguishable templates and lower-bounds their ordinary normalized L2 distance, but Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 use an infimum over deformations, D. A lower bound on ordinary L2 distance does not imply D is of order 1/d; D could be much smaller. A formal minimax result stated in terms of D is needed.

There are additional proof gaps. Section 4 emphasizes that deformations need not be invertible, but Proposition B.4 assumes support(f composed with A) is contained in the image and Equation (90) uses a one-to-one change-of-variables equality, neither of which follows from Assumption 2(i) for a non-injective A. The proof of Lemma A.7 incorrectly infers a positive neighborhood at a support boundary, Theorem 3.8 uses xi*xi' rather than sqrt(xi*xi') in an L2 change of variables, and Theorem 4.4 mishandles threshold ties through its sign-based error equality. Some may be repairable, but they affect central stated results as written.

Significance and evidence: The experiments generate every sample by transforming a single handpicked image per class, almost exactly instantiating the assumed model. They do not test natural within-class variation, noise, clutter, occlusion, or standard train/test splits. There are no meaningful baselines, uncertainty intervals, resolution/separation experiments, or tests of the predicted dependence on deformation-cover size. Thus the experiments demonstrate that synthetic augmentation is learnable rather than corroborating the main rates or practical relevance.

The experimental CNNs do not clearly instantiate the architecture used in the theory, and the manuscript does not verify the Lipschitz, visibility, covering, or separation assumptions for any experiment. The statement that larger empirical networks improve because they provide a finer approximation to the deformation set is therefore speculative.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript provides no code and omits template identifiers, augmentation ranges and distributions, foreground-extraction details, random seeds, epochs, batch size, initialization, stopping rules, full layer specifications, and inverse-mapping implementation details. Table 1 and the optimizer learning rate are insufficient to reproduce Figures 9-11.

Originality is moderate rather than commensurate with the title's claim of a novel framework. Template-orbit models, registration/alignment, invariant representations, and translation invariance from convolution plus global pooling are established ideas; the main novelty is the particular statistical analysis under a highly specialized noiseless model.

Some claims exceed the results: 0-1 ERM softmax outputs are called estimates of conditional probabilities without a calibration result, noise robustness is justified only by an informal CLT argument, and connections to overparameterization and data augmentation are suggested but not analyzed. Overall, the substantial theoretical effort is promising, but the metric mismatch, proof gaps, weak empirical validation, and poor reproducibility outweigh the merits in the present version.

strengths: Soundness in the restricted setting: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 give precise sufficient conditions for perfect classification under invertible or axis-aligned deformations, with detailed proofs connecting pixelization error, alignment, and the O(1/d) separation scale.

Originality: Treating pixel count as image resolution rather than ambient dimension is an interesting statistical perspective. The orbit-based separation quantities and connection between deformation covers and CNN architecture provide useful conceptual insights.
Significance: The explicit CNN construction and VC-based bounds in Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 offer a nontrivial bridge between invariance, approximation, deformation complexity, and generalization.

Presentation: The model and algorithms are generally explained clearly, with helpful figures and extensive proofs. The discussion relates the work thoughtfully to pattern theory, functional-data registration, scattering transforms, and equivariant networks.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly discusses backgrounds, occlusion, multiple objects, perspective changes, sharp edges, and the gap between ERM and practical optimization. Its use of standard image benchmarks raises no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed removal of invertibility from the CNN theory is unsupported as written. Proposition B.4 and the proof around equations (90)-(100) require properties such as supp(f composed with A) being contained in the image domain and valid change-of-variables arguments. Assumption 2(i), which only requires the template support to lie in A([0,1]^2) and bounds derivatives, does not imply these properties for non-injective A. This affects Theorem 4.2 and consequently Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 unless stronger injectivity or support-preimage assumptions are added.

Soundness: Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between two indistinguishable templates, but it does not lower-bound the orbit separation D used by the upper bounds. It therefore does not establish the stated optimality of the O(1/d) condition on D. Its proof also writes a change-of-variables factor as xi times xi-prime rather than its square root, although the final lower bound appears repairable.

Significance: Every class is represented by one deterministic template, and all variability is assumed to be a label-independent geometric deformation with no observation noise, fully visible objects, and essentially zero background. Natural within-class variation cannot generally be represented this way; this central limitation is not addressed as directly as the secondary extensions discussed in Section 7.

Evidence: The experiments select one image per class and generate both training and test sets by deforming those same images. This exactly matches the assumed model and does not evaluate ordinary within-class variation. They neither vary resolution nor measure D or deformation-cover complexity, and the practical 10-by-10-filter CNNs are not quantitatively connected to the architecture or bounds in Section 4. Thus the experiments do not substantiate the broader theoretical claims.

Reproducibility: No code is provided, and essential details are absent, including augmentation ranges and distributions, exact template identifiers and preprocessing, random seeds, epochs, batch sizes, dense-layer counts, and stopping criteria. Only medians from 10 repetitions with small test sets are reported, without uncertainty. Equation (37) also uses inconsistent test-set indexing.

Presentation and applicability: Assumption 3 is awkwardly stated and is not formally verified for the concrete affine deformation families whose covering cardinalities are asserted. The 30-page main text is substantially overlong for the ICML format, while several technical slips remain, including the strict-threshold/tie mismatch in equation (125).

strengths: Originality/significance: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ab3d7mqx/call-3eb8569fdd7b413e95707c670eb5a044/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} offers an interesting functional-data perspective in which within-class image variability arises from latent geometric deformations rather than generic high-dimensional noise.

Soundness: Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 carefully quantify pixelization error and give explicit sufficient separation conditions for perfect classification by inverse-mapping and alignment-based nearest-neighbor rules.

The CNN analysis is technically ambitious: Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 combine an explicit invariant network construction with VC-dimension or entropy arguments to obtain sample-size bounds for both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.
Presentation: The definitions, assumptions, connections to registration, scattering, and functional data analysis, and most proof steps are explained in substantial detail.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly acknowledges the optimization gap and limitations involving noise, complex backgrounds, occlusion, multiple objects, and sharp edges. The standard benchmark imagery raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline claim that the O(1/d) separation condition is necessary is not established as written. Theorem 3.8 states that fixed templates work for every sufficiently large d, but its proof constructs the perturbation—and hence f1—using d. Moreover, it lower-bounds ordinary ||f1-f0|| rather than the deformation-invariant separation D from (12)/(23); because D takes an infimum over transformations, the former does not imply D=Omega(1/d). Thus the claimed matching lower bound for Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 is missing.

The proof of Theorem 3.8 also uses the incorrect change-of-variables identity ||f1-f0||_2=xi xi' ||g||_2 instead of sqrt(xi xi')||g||_2. The final order appears repairable, but it adds to the need for theorem-level revision.

Significance is limited by the generative assumptions: each class has one fixed template, labels are deterministic given the image, backgrounds are exactly zero, objects are fully visible, and there is no additive noise or within-class variation beyond the stipulated deformation family. These assumptions largely create the zero-Bayes-error setting underlying the perfect-classification results.

Assumption 3 is crucial to the CNN results, yet the claimed covering cardinalities for the motivating scaling/affine deformation classes are asserted rather than formally verified. The multi-class extension is likewise only sketched.

Evaluation: Every task selects one image per class and generates all training and test examples by synthetic transformations of those same two templates. There are no real within-class splits, generic baselines, uncertainty intervals, or controlled experiments varying image resolution, separation, or deformation-cover complexity. Consequently, Figures 9–11 do not convincingly corroborate the stated rates or broader image-classification claims.

Theory and experiments are poorly matched: the guarantees concern global ERM over a bounded, block-structured architecture tied to a deformation cover, whereas the experiments train ordinary 10x10-filter CNNs with Adam. No argument connects these trained models to the analyzed estimator.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code, and the manuscript omits exact deformation ranges, selected template identifiers, random seeds, batch size, epochs or stopping rule, and a complete experimental architecture specification. Overall, the promising upper-bound theory is outweighed by the unresolved lower-bound claim and weak empirical support.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ddxeqgbk/call-c3671a47b5664aca933e748811dec525/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} gives a precise deformation-based generative model and substantial constructive analysis. The sufficient-condition results for inverse mapping, alignment, and CNN realizability explicitly track image resolution, template regularity, and deformation-cover complexity.

Originality: Viewing resolution as increasingly accurate observation of a deformed function, rather than simply increasing ambient dimension, is a useful perspective. Connecting this model to explicit CNN filters and distribution-free ERM bounds provides some new understanding even though the individual ingredients are familiar.

Significance: The dependence on deformation-set covering numbers is informative, and the affine, rotation, scaling, and wave-deformation examples make the abstract framework more concrete. The distinction between nuisance deformation and additive observation noise is conceptually valuable.
Presentation: The paper is generally readable, carefully organized, and supported by useful diagrams. The extensive appendices expose most proof details rather than hiding key arguments.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion candidly acknowledges computationally infeasible inverse search, idealized ERM optimization, background noise, occlusion, partial visibility, and multiple objects. No material ethical concern is apparent for this theoretical study using public benchmark imagery and synthetic transformations.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 3.8 does not establish the claimed matching lower bound for Theorems 3.1 and 3.7. It bounds the ordinary normalized distance between f0 and f1, but never shows that the relevant deformation-invariant separation D—an infimum over transformations—is of order 1/d. Page 50 also uses an incorrect L2 scaling factor ξξ′ rather than sqrt(ξξ′); the coarse numerical conclusion may be repairable, but the stated optimality claim is unsupported.

Soundness: Equation (125) in the proof of Theorem 4.4 incorrectly equates classification error with P(sign(k p(X))<0). Because prediction uses the strict rule 1(p(X)>0), a positive-class tie p(X)=0 is also an error. No zero-tie assumption is given, so the cross-entropy theorem is not proved as stated.

Significance: The central model assumes one noiseless template per class, exact prescribed deformations, global brightness variation, zero background, full object visibility, and zero Bayes error. Real intra-class appearance, texture, viewpoint, clutter, and sensor variation are excluded; the proposed noisy and multi-object extensions remain speculative.

The CNN guarantees concern global ERM over a specially constrained architecture whose constructive filters depend on the unknown templates and a deformation cover. They do not explain whether gradient training finds such a solution. The Adam-trained 10×10-filter networks in Section 5 are not matched to the block-structured architecture or cover size used in the proofs.

Evaluation: Every task is generated by repeatedly deforming just one selected image per class. Thus the experiments test recovery of two fixed template orbits, not classification on MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet distributions. There are no competitive baselines, noise or intra-class stress tests, separation estimates, resolution sweeps, or deformation-complexity sweeps, so the principal theoretical predictions are not empirically validated.

Reproducibility: No code is supplied, and the deformation ranges, selected image identifiers, random seeds, epochs, batch sizes, stopping rules, and several preprocessing details are absent. Results report only medians over 10 repetitions with 50 or 200 test examples and no uncertainty intervals.

Originality and presentation: Registration/alignment plus nearest-neighbor classification, template-correlation filters with global pooling, and VC-based ERM bounds are established ideas. The manuscript's synthesis has merit, but its novelty relative to invariant/equivariant learning and orbit-based classification is not isolated sharply; the unusually long exposition and late placement of related work further obscure the core contribution. Overall, the valid sufficient-condition results are promising, but the unresolved lower-bound claim, cross-entropy proof gap, and weak evidence require major revision before the contribution can be relied upon.

strengths: The paper offers a coherent continuous-template perspective that separates image resolution from deformation complexity and connects functional data analysis, registration, invariant representations, and CNN classification. This is a potentially useful theoretical direction. The complete manuscript was reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-7aevebhp/call-54c0d123fd7b44b0b99529fe64c715d8/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers are precisely defined, and Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 provide interpretable sufficient conditions relating pixel resolution, deformation regularity, and class separation. Extensive proofs make many assumptions and constants traceable.

The matched-filter CNN construction and its combination with VC-dimension and entropy arguments are technically interesting. Treating both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM, and discussing multiclass extensions, gives the theoretical contribution useful breadth.

The manuscript is generally clear despite its length. Figures 3-7 explain the geometric intuition effectively, and the literature discussion appropriately relates the work to deformable templates, scattering, registration, and group-equivariant networks.

The authors candidly acknowledge the inverse method's computational cost, the gap between ERM and gradient-based optimization, and the absence of theory for noise, structured backgrounds, occlusion, and multiple objects. The primarily theoretical work and synthetic transformations of established benchmarks raise no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The model assumes that every image in a class is an exact brightness-scaled geometric deformation of one fixed, noiseless, nonnegative template with a zero background and full visibility. Consequently, one example per class can suffice largely by construction. It excludes the within-class appearance, pose, texture, background, sensor-noise, and instance variation central to real image classification, substantially limiting significance.

The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established for the paper's actual separation metric. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds only the unaligned distance ||f1-f0||/||f0|| for an indistinguishable pair, whereas the guarantees use D from Equation (23), an infimum over brightness, scaling, and translation. Since D is at most the unaligned distance, the theorem provides no lower bound on D and therefore does not justify the repeated claim that the D-based condition is necessary or optimal.

The advertised extension to non-invertible deformations is not supported by the stated proof. Proposition B.4 and the proof of Proposition B.5 infer that supp(f composed with A) lies in the image domain, assert f(A(0,0))=0, and use a change-of-variables equality in Equation (90). These properties do not follow from Assumption 2(i) for a general non-injective map; such maps may also make the R2 separation norms in Equation (32) non-finite. Additional support, properness, or multiplicity assumptions are required.

The CNN guarantees concern exact global ERM over the specially defined class G, and the existence proof uses matched filters determined by the unknown templates and a deformation cover. The experiments instead train materially different 10-by-10 CNNs with Adam. No argument connects Adam's output or the architectures in Table 1 to the theoretical estimator, so Figures 10-11 do not corroborate Theorems 4.1 or 4.4.

The empirical evaluation is too weak for the claims: train and test images are merely augmentations of the same single selected image per class, there are no ordinary held-out instances, standard baselines, robustness tests, resolution or separation sweeps, cover-complexity tests, uncertainty intervals, or ablations. Median errors from only 10 repetitions and 50 or 200 test examples provide limited evidence, and the claim that wider networks yield a finer approximation of the deformation set is not directly tested.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no code or configuration, and the paper omits template-image identifiers, deformation ranges and distributions, preprocessing details, epochs, batch size, initialization, stopping criteria, and random seeds. The inverse-mapping grids are also insufficiently specified to reconstruct the experiments.

The bounds can require n to exceed a deformation-cover-dependent parameter count growing rapidly with resolution, but the paper never instantiates them in the experimental regimes or shows that they are non-vacuous. Likewise, the statement that the V/n rate is minimax optimal is cited from generic VC theory without a lower bound for this deformation model. As supplied, the 81-page author-identified arXiv document is also not in anonymous ICML submission format. These technical, evidential, and reproducibility issues require substantially more than a minor revision.
