strengths: Originality/significance: The continuous-template deformation model offers an interesting statistical perspective on image classification, clarifying how greater pixel resolution can improve separability rather than merely increase ambient dimension.

Soundness: The inverse-mapping and alignment analyses give explicit assumptions and constructive sufficient conditions for perfect classification, including careful treatment of pixelization error and nuisance brightness, translation, and scaling.
The CNN section usefully connects deformation-covering complexity, network construction, and VC/entropy arguments to derive realizable-case bounds for both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.

Presentation: The manuscript is largely self-contained, extensively proved, visually legible, and well connected to registration, functional data analysis, scattering transforms, and equivariant learning. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8feynebf/call-d564f5dc8b2c4537a0188922dc4c3288/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Limitations and ethics: The conclusion candidly identifies background noise, structured scenes, occlusion, multiple objects, sharp edges, perspective, and optimization as unresolved. The synthetic/public-benchmark study raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The advertised necessity of the 1/d separation rate is not established as written. Theorem 3.8 bounds the ordinary unregistered L2 distance rather than the separation quantity D in (23), and states no matching O(1/d) upper bound. Moreover, its quantifiers assert fixed templates working for every sufficiently large d, whereas the proof constructs f1 through a perturbation g that depends on d and on the chosen deformation parameters.

The CNN results claim to cover non-invertible deformations under Assumption 2(i), but key proof steps use properties that this assumption does not imply: supp(f composed with A) contained in the image square, f(A(0,0))=0 in Proposition B.4, and an unqualified change-of-variables identity in (90). The theorem therefore needs stronger injectivity/preimage assumptions or a substantially revised proof.

The cross-entropy proof has an unresolved tie issue: (125) equates error of the strict threshold q2>1/2 with the event sgn(kf)<0, which omits f=0 for positive-class examples; subsequent equalities, including (128), rely on that equivalence without a no-ties condition.

The evaluation is almost entirely assumption-confirming: each class is generated by repeatedly deforming one selected template, often after replacing the natural background with black. It therefore excludes genuine within-class shape variation, sensor/background noise, clutter, occlusion, and multiple objects—the phenomena that determine usefulness for real image classification.

Experiments do not test the central predicted dependence on resolution d, separation D, or deformation-covering size. The implemented 10x10-filter Adam-trained CNNs also differ materially from the full-image, block-structured filters and ideal ERM analyzed in the theory, so Figure 11 does not validate Theorems 4.1 or 4.4.

Reproducibility is inadequate: deformation distributions and parameter ranges, exact selected templates, background-removal procedure, epochs, batch sizes, stopping criteria, and random seeds are omitted; no code is supplied. Reporting only medians over 10 runs with 50 or 200 test examples and no uncertainty further limits evidential value.

The practical reach is narrow: the strongest guarantees assume noiseless exact template orbits, full visibility, zero background, known deformation structure, and global empirical-risk minimization. The 30-page main text is also considerably longer than necessary, with some notation and test-set indexing inconsistencies. Overall, the promising theoretical viewpoint is not yet supported reliably enough for acceptance.

strengths: [Soundness] The manuscript formulates a precise deformation-based generative model and states explicit smoothness, visibility, separation, and deformation-complexity assumptions. Theorems 3.1, 3.7, 4.1, and 4.4 are accompanied by substantial proofs. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-f63t4r3a/call-5a6fe86ef1cb49d8bc3408ce2e255895/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

[Significance] The near-matching resolution-dependent separation results around 1/d provide a useful finite-pixel perspective: increasing resolution can improve identifiability rather than merely increase ambient dimension.

[Originality] The main novelty is a coherent theoretical synthesis connecting deformation orbits, image alignment, template-matching CNN filters, deformation covering numbers, and statistical generalization bounds.
[Presentation] The definitions and high-level arguments are generally clear, figures aid intuition, and the extensive appendix makes the theory comparatively auditable.

[Limitations and ethics] Section 7 candidly identifies unhandled backgrounds, noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and sharp edges. The work uses established image benchmarks and presents no apparent material ethical risk.
weaknesses: [Soundness] The main CNN results are not justified under their stated assumptions. Propositions B.4-B.5 repeatedly infer supp(f composed with A) is contained in [0,1]^2 from Assumption 2(i), but this implication requires injectivity; the paper explicitly claims on page 19 that CNN results allow non-invertible deformations. Equation (90) likewise uses an injective change-of-variables equality under only Assumption 2(i). Consequently, Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 require an additional invertibility/support-containment condition or a revised proof.

[Soundness] Several further proof-level inaccuracies reduce confidence: Lemma 3.5 does not establish a finite order-d^2 cover by its stated absolute discretization because lambda is unbounded; the proof of Theorem 3.8 uses xi times xi-prime rather than its square root as the L2 change-of-variables factor; and equations (125) and (128) mishandle zero-logit ties. These look repairable but should be corrected before acceptance.

[Significance] The model assumes one fixed, noiseless template per class, zero background, full visibility, and label-independent transformations. Perfect classification from one example per class largely follows from disjoint noiseless deformation orbits and does not address natural intra-class semantic variation, clutter, sensor noise, or occlusion. The honest discussion of these limitations is welcome, but they substantially restrict the conclusions.

[Evaluation] All data are synthetic transformations of one selected exemplar per class. There are no raw-pixel nearest-neighbor, conventional CNN, augmentation, registration, scattering, or group-equivariant baselines; resolution and separation are not varied; and only medians over 10 runs with 50 or 200 test examples are shown, without uncertainty. Thus the experiments do not convincingly corroborate the predicted rates or broader image-classification claims.

[Theory-practice connection] The guarantees concern ideal global ERM over a custom architecture whose constructive filters encode transformed templates, whereas the experiments use 10-by-10 filters trained with Adam. No argument verifies that the implemented networks match the theoretical class, attain the ERM, or satisfy the separation and covering assumptions.

[Reproducibility] No code is supplied, and the manuscript omits template-image identifiers, transformation ranges and distributions, random seeds, detailed preprocessing, batch size, epochs, initialization, stopping criteria, and a complete implemented architecture. The experiments therefore cannot be reliably reproduced.

[Originality] Template deformation models, alignment, matched filtering, and invariant representations are established ideas; after the existential CNN construction, the learning rate mainly follows from a standard realizable-case VC bound. The claim that the V/n rate is minimax optimal is not supported by a lower bound for this deformation model.

[Ethics] There is no explicit ethics/impact statement or provenance and licensing discussion for the selected ImageNet examples. This is a minor documentation issue rather than a decisive ethical concern.

attempts.developer_message:
Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

Originality and significance: The paper offers a useful statistical perspective in which within-class randomness arises from geometric deformation rather than additive noise. Its explicit dependence on deformation-cover complexity, resolution, and sample size advances theoretical understanding of invariant classification.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript is generally well organized and places the work thoughtfully among pattern theory, functional-data registration, scattering transforms, and invariant networks. It candidly acknowledges the inverse method's computational cost, the gap between ERM and gradient-based optimization, and difficulties involving backgrounds, occlusion, and multiple objects.
No material research-ethics concern is apparent: the experiments use standard public image sources to create synthetic deformation tasks, and the theoretical contribution is low risk.
weaknesses: The model is highly restrictive: every class has one fixed, noiseless, nonnegative template, and all within-class variability is label-preserving deformation with zero background and full visibility. It excludes genuine intra-class appearance variation, structured backgrounds, noise, occlusion, and multiple objects, so the striking one-sample-per-class recovery result has limited relevance to ordinary image classification.

The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established for the paper's actual separation quantity. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the raw normalized L2 distance between f0 and f1, whereas D in (12) and (23) is an infimum over brightness, scaling, shifts, and deformations; a lower bound on raw distance does not lower-bound D. Its proof also uses ξξ′ rather than the correct square-root Jacobian factor when transforming an L2 norm, although correcting this appears to preserve the rate.

The central CNN results remain conditional on Assumption 3. The manuscript informally states covering cardinalities for scaling and affine/rotation families but does not rigorously verify this unusual shift-adjusted assumption for those classes or derive concrete corollaries, leaving the advertised dimension dependence difficult to validate.

There is a substantial theory-experiment disconnect. The expressivity proof uses template-matched, block-structured filters and ideal global ERM, whereas the experiments use 10×10 filters trained with Adam; no result connects that optimizer or experimental architecture to the theoretical witness. The manuscript honestly notes the optimization limitation, but it prevents the experiments from validating the theorem.

The empirical evidence is weak: each binary task is generated from only one selected source image per class and train/test images are synthetic augmentations of those same two templates. Results report medians over ten runs with only 50 or 200 test examples, without uncertainty intervals, standard baselines, resolution or separation ablations, or tests of the predicted deformation-cover/sample-size rates.

Empirical reproducibility is inadequate. No code is supplied, and the manuscript omits template identifiers, augmentation ranges and distributions, random seeds, batch size, epoch count, stopping rule, several architectural details, and the precise inverse-mapping grids and preprocessing steps.

Equation (125) equates threshold-classification error with a strict negative-margin event, but this fails for a zero logit on a positive-class example unless zero-probability ties are established; no such assumption is made. This appears repairable, but Theorem 4.4 is not proved exactly as stated.

Although readable, the 30-page main discussion and 81-page total manuscript are overly long for the ICML main track, and several notation inconsistencies and typographical errors further hinder presentation. Overall, the promising theory requires correction, concrete instantiation, and substantially stronger reproducible evidence before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Originality: The deformation-orbit perspective offers a coherent alternative to treating pixels as unrelated covariates, and the analysis usefully highlights how increasing resolution can improve identifiability.

Soundness: The upper-bound program is mathematically substantial. The inverse-mapping, alignment, and CNN results are supported by explicit constructions, separation conditions, discretization arguments, and extensive proofs rather than informal intuition alone.

Significance: Connecting deformation covers, template separation, CNN filter complexity, and VC/entropy generalization bounds could provide a useful starting point for statistical theories of invariant classification.

Presentation: The assumptions and theorem statements are generally clear, and the figures help explain alignment and template-filter matching. The manuscript is largely self-contained :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-kft3tuz1/call-58c42ba9706d4019b401e76a0fee6ee7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly acknowledge computationally impractical inverse search, idealized ERM optimization, and omitted background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and perspective effects. The experiments use standard image datasets and synthetic transformations, with no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established in the paper's actual deformation-invariant distance D. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds only the ordinary normalized L2 distance between f0 and f1; it does not show D(f0,f1) or D(f1,f0) is of order 1/d. Moreover, f1 is constructed after fixing a particular deformation tuple. Thus the repeated assertion that the sufficient D condition is necessary does not follow as written.

Soundness: The CNN theorems advertise applicability without invertible deformations, but Appendix B uses properties not supplied by Assumption 2(i). In particular, it asserts that supp(f composed with A) lies in the image domain and uses a change-of-variables equality in (90); these are generally invalid for a non-injective A under the stated assumptions. The advertised generality therefore needs stronger assumptions or a revised proof.

Significance: The realizable model permits exactly one noiseless template per class, with within-class variability arising only from prescribed geometric transformations and brightness. It excludes the shape, texture, background, viewpoint, and semantic variation that dominate real image classification, so perfect classification from one example per class has limited external meaning.

Evidence: The experiments do not use the natural variability of MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet. They select one image per class and synthesize both training and test sets from that same template, making the evaluation closely match—and largely trivialize—the assumed model.

Evidence: The numerical study does not test the central rates or assumptions: it does not vary resolution d systematically, estimate the separation D, vary deformation-cover complexity, or compare observed scaling with bounds. It also lacks standard baselines such as ordinary nearest neighbors, registration methods, augmented CNNs, or group-equivariant models.

Theory–experiment mismatch: The analyzed CNN is an exhaustive template/deformation filter bank with block-structured, potentially image-sized filters and specially constructed max networks. The experiments instead use learned 10-by-10 filters and generic fully connected layers. Their success cannot corroborate the proposed CNN construction or its bounds.

Optimization: Both CNN guarantees concern global empirical-risk minimizers. Cross-entropy does not make optimization over this nonconvex architecture tractable, and the discussion of unrelated overparameterized regimes does not show that Adam reaches the required estimator. The practical algorithm is therefore outside the theory.

Reproducibility: No code is provided, and essential details are missing, including selected template-image identifiers, deformation ranges and distributions, random seeds, batch size, epoch count or stopping rule, initialization, exact layer layout, and inverse-grid construction.

Evaluation reliability: Results report only medians over 10 repetitions with test sets of merely 50 or 200 examples, without dispersion or confidence intervals. Near-zero errors therefore have coarse resolution and uncertain stability.

Presentation and scope: At 81 pages, the manuscript is disproportionately long for the empirical and conceptual scope. Several broad claims about practical CNN behavior and near-perfect image classification exceed what the highly idealized model and synthetic evidence establish. Overall, substantive theoretical clarification and a much stronger evaluation are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The continuous-template and pixel-averaging model is explicit, and Section 3 provides detailed, largely self-contained arguments showing how discretization or alignment error scales as O(1/d). :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-0yitlrow/call-a3896645845646f68591d2084de92b50/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Originality: Recasting image classification as classification of deformation orbits, then connecting explicit matched-filter CNN constructions to statistical generalization bounds, is an interesting synthesis of functional data analysis, registration, and neural-network theory.

Significance: The dependence on deformation-cover complexity rather than treating all d^2 pixels as unrelated variables offers a potentially useful structural perspective on image-classification theory.
Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, motivates the constructions intuitively, and includes helpful illustrations and extensive proofs.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly discuss optimization, noise, structured backgrounds, multiple objects, occlusion, and more complex transformations. The work uses standard benchmark data in low-risk synthetic experiments, with no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The CNN theorems are not established under their stated assumptions. Proposition B.4 and the proof of Proposition B.5 assert that supp(f composed with A) is contained in [0,1]^2 and use an injective-style change of variables, while Section 4 explicitly permits non-invertible deformations and Assumption 2(i) provides only regularity and visibility. Folding or periodic maps can satisfy those conditions while creating additional preimages; the L2(R^2) separation in (32) may then be ill-defined. Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 require stronger invertibility/proper-support assumptions or a substantially revised proof.

The claimed optimality result is incomplete. Theorem 3.8 states that fixed f0 and f1 work for every sufficiently large d, but its construction makes the perturbation—and hence f1—depend on d. Moreover, it lower-bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between f0 and f1, not the deformation-orbit separation D in (23). It therefore does not establish that the sufficient D of order 1/d condition is necessary.

The model assumes one noiseless, nonnegative template per class, exact geometric deformation, zero background, full visibility, and a known deformation class. Under separation the label is deterministic and Bayes error is zero. These assumptions omit most natural within-class semantic variation, so the broad implications claimed for practical image classification and near-perfect deep-learning performance are not supported.

The evaluation uses only random augmentations of one selected exemplar per class, with test samples generated by the identical augmentation pipeline. This directly instantiates the easiest orbit model rather than testing ordinary MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet classification. There are no standard, registration, scattering, or equivariant baselines and no experiments varying resolution, separation, or covering number to test the quantitative theory.

The experimental CNNs use learned 10-by-10 filters and jointly change filter count and dense-layer width, whereas the proof constructs highly specialized template/deformation filters with a particular max-computation network and assumes exact ERM. Consequently, Figure 11 does not specifically validate the proposed architecture, approximation mechanism, or rate.

Empirical reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code link, and the manuscript omits template identifiers, deformation ranges and distributions, masking/thresholding details, inverse-map grids and parameter ranges, training epochs, batch size, stopping rule, initialization, and seeds. Reporting medians over only ten repetitions with N=50 or 200 and no uncertainty further limits evidential value.

Much of the machinery—alignment, registration, orbit matching, matched filters, and realizable-case VC bounds—is established. The new synthesis is promising, but the V/n result is largely inherited from standard learning theory, may involve very large deformation covers, and lacks a model-specific minimax lower bound.

Despite generally clear exposition, the 30-page main text is not concise for an ICML submission, and several imprecise statements—including the quantifiers in Theorem 3.8 and the test-set indexing in Section 5—make verification harder. The technical and empirical issues require major revision before others can reliably build on the central claims.

attempts.developer_message:
Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: Soundness: Within the explicitly noiseless, single-template deformation model, the paper develops concrete inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers and derives interpretable finite-resolution guarantees. The CNN analysis also connects deformation-covering complexity, architecture size, and sample complexity, with extensive proofs supplied in the appendix.

Originality: Treating increased pixel resolution as beneficial discretization of a structured functional object, rather than simply increased ambient dimension, is a useful perspective. The attempt to derive deformation-dependent CNN rates provides some new theoretical understanding even though alignment and template-orbit models themselves are classical.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, defines its notation carefully, and uses helpful illustrations to explain deformation, alignment, and filter matching. The relationship to functional registration, scattering transforms, and group-equivariant methods is discussed.

Limitations and ethics: Sections 4.2 and 7 candidly acknowledge the optimization gap, background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and richer deformations. The experiments use established image datasets and raise no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The stated scope of the CNN theorems is not fully supported. Assumption 2(i) only places the template support inside A([0,1]^2); for a non-injective A, it does not imply that the support of f composed with A is contained in [0,1]^2. Nevertheless, Propositions B.4-B.5 repeatedly use that implication, and Eq. (90) writes a change-of-variables equality that generally requires injectivity or a multiplicity correction. This is especially consequential because Section 4 explicitly claims that invertibility is unnecessary. Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 need stronger support/properness assumptions or a revised proof.

Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation condition is not established as stated. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary L2 distance between f0 and f1, whereas the sufficient results use the orbit-based quantity D, an infimum over rescalings, shifts, and brightness; no corresponding lower bound on D is proved. Moreover, the theorem's quantifiers suggest fixed templates valid for every d, while its construction makes f1 depend on d. The proof on page 50 also uses a factor ξξ′ where L2 change of variables gives sqrt(ξξ′), although the final numerical bound appears repairable.

Significance: The data model assumes every image in a class is exactly a deformation of one fixed template, with no within-class appearance variation, observation noise, structured background, cropping, or multiple objects. Under these assumptions the label is deterministic and one example per class can suffice, so the perfect-classification conclusion is substantially built into the model and does not explain ordinary image classification datasets.

Evidence: The experiments generate both training and test samples by augmenting one selected image per class. They therefore test interpolation within the assumed template orbit, not classification across naturally varying MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet instances. There are no relevant baselines, out-of-model perturbations, uncertainty intervals, or tests of the stated separation and rate dependence; N=50 or 200 and medians over ten repetitions provide weak evidence for claims of convergence to zero.

Theory-experiment mismatch: The theoretical construction uses template-derived, block-structured, potentially full-image filters, with 2|A_d| filters and ideal empirical-risk minimization. Table 1 instead evaluates learned 10x10-filter networks trained by Adam. The deformation-covering size, α, separation D, theoretical depth, and predicted rates are never instantiated, so Figure 11 does not substantively corroborate Theorems 4.1 or 4.4, nor does merely increasing width demonstrate a finer deformation covering.

Reproducibility: No code is provided, and essential experimental details are missing: exact augmentation distributions and ranges, template identities and splits, preprocessing and background removal, interpolation and thresholding rules, inverse-map grids, fully connected depth, epochs, batch size, stopping criteria, software versions, and random seeds. Table 1 is insufficient to reconstruct the reported CNNs.

Originality and practical utility: Template-orbit models, registration, and invariant representations are well established. The new analysis is specialized, while the inverse-mapping classifier is acknowledged to be computationally demanding and the CNN results concern an unavailable global ERM. Consequently, the manuscript currently offers limited actionable guidance for realistic classifiers. These technical, evidential, and reproducibility issues outweigh the conceptual merits, although the core direction is substantial enough for a weak rather than strong rejection.

strengths: Soundness: The paper defines a coherent generative model based on pixelized, randomly deformed Lipschitz templates and provides constructive analyses for inverse-mapping, alignment, and CNN classifiers. The extensive appendices make assumptions and proof steps unusually inspectable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-9eeu4oih/call-6ee847d3ab9448aabccb8d86c9f4b187/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Originality/significance: Relating image resolution, orbit separation, deformation-cover cardinality, CNN size, and misclassification risk offers a useful statistical perspective distinct from treating pixels as unrelated covariates.

Presentation: The progression from the general model to specialized alignment and then CNN ERM is logical. Concrete affine and nonlinear examples, illustrations, and an explicit discussion of the optimization gap aid understanding.

Limitations/ethics: The authors candidly discuss zero backgrounds, noise, occlusion, multiple objects, sharp edges, perspective transformations, and the lack of optimization guarantees. No material ethical concern is apparent for this theoretical study using synthetically transformed benchmark images.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed optimality of the 1/d separation rate is not established for the paper's actual separation quantity. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds only the ordinary normalized L2 distance between f0 and f1, whereas Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 use an infimum over transformations and intensity rescalings. Since that orbit distance can be substantially smaller, the assertion that Theorem 3.8 proves necessity for D does not follow. Its proof also uses the incorrect L2 change-of-variables factor ξξ′ instead of sqrt(ξξ′), although the final order may be repairable.

Soundness/scope: Theorems 4.1–4.2 are stated using Assumption 2(i), and the text explicitly claims invertibility is unnecessary, yet Proposition B.5 uses a change-of-variables identity and support containment for f composed with A that are not implied for general non-injective maps. The theorem needs stronger assumptions or a revised area-formula/truncation argument. Equation (125) also omits zero-margin positive-class ties by using a strict sign inequality.

Technical completeness: Lemma 3.5 allows unbounded |λ| but claims an O(d²) finite cover by discretizing λ at resolution O(1/d); that construction would require infinitely many grid points. Discretizing 1/λ could plausibly repair the result, but that argument is absent.

Evidence: Experiments generate every class from only one chosen template and the same simple transformations assumed by the theory. They therefore omit natural within-class variation, cluttered backgrounds, noise, and partial visibility. They do not test the central predicted dependence on resolution d, separation D, or deformation-cover complexity, and include no registration, equivariant-CNN, scattering, or ordinary-CNN baselines. Medians over ten repetitions without uncertainty are weak validation.

Reproducibility: Exact augmentation ranges/distributions, selected template identifiers, preprocessing details, seeds, batch sizes, epoch counts, stopping rules, and code are not provided. Consequently, Figures 9 and 11 cannot be reliably reproduced.

Significance: The CNN results concern ideal global ERM and rely on existence of template-matched filters; the 0–1 ERM is computationally intractable, while the Adam experiments use a different practical architecture without any link to the optimization theory. Combined with the highly noiseless fixed-template model, this substantially limits what the results establish about realistic image classification.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript develops a mathematically explicit deformation model and states clear separation conditions. The finite-resolution analysis in Theorems 3.1, 3.7, and 3.8 is an interesting way to formalize pixelization and non-identifiability, and extensive proofs are provided.

Originality and significance: Connecting functional-data deformation models, image alignment, and CNN generalization is a potentially useful synthesis. The explicit dependence on deformation covering numbers offers more structural insight than treating all pixels as unrelated covariates.

Presentation: The progression from generative model to alignment classifiers and CNNs is coherent, and the diagrams make the constructions understandable. The authors also candidly acknowledge computational infeasibility of inverse mapping, fragility to background noise, and the absence of optimization guarantees.
Ethics: No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the work is theoretical and uses established benchmark images to create synthetic examples.
weaknesses: Soundness and scope: Every class is represented by one deterministic template, and all variability is an exact deformation plus brightness scaling. There is no background or sensor noise, intrinsic within-class variation, clutter, occlusion, or label ambiguity. Under the separation assumption the Bayes error is forced to zero, so perfect classification from one example per class has limited bearing on realistic image classification.

Evidence: Sections 5.1–5.2 do not evaluate FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet classification in the usual sense. One image per class is selected and both training and test sets are transformations of those same images, sometimes after imposing black backgrounds. Figures 9–11 therefore test an artificially favorable matched-template problem and do not support broader claims about object recognition.

The experiments do not test the theoretical predictions quantitatively: resolution d, separation D, and deformation-covering complexity are not varied; no predicted rate is fitted; and no raw-pixel nearest-neighbor, registration, standard CNN, augmentation, or equivariant-network baseline is included. Increasing filter count and fully connected width simultaneously also does not establish the claimed mechanism of finer deformation approximation. Test sets of only 50 or 200 examples and medians over ten runs without dispersion further weaken the evidence.

There is a substantial theory–practice disconnect. Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 concern global empirical-risk minimizers over a specially sized architecture, while the experiments use Adam. The separator constructed in Theorem 4.2 is effectively an exhaustive bank of filters derived from the unknown templates and a deformation cover, whereas Table 1 uses learned 10-by-10 filters with no demonstrated correspondence to that construction.

Several proof details require correction. Equation (90) invokes a change-of-variables equality although Section 4 assumes only Assumption 2(i) and explicitly advertises non-invertible deformations; multiplicity must be handled with an area formula. Lemma 3.5 claims a finite order-d-squared cover by discretizing an unbounded wavelength parameter with order-1/d absolute spacing. Equations (125)–(128) also omit classification errors occurring at zero-logit ties. Some conclusions may be repairable, but the advertised generality is not established as written.

Significance is limited by the construction and rates. Once an oracle matched-filter separator is established, the sample bound is largely a standard realizable VC/entropy argument; for rotation plus scaling, the stated covering heuristic gives |A_dα| on the order of d^(3α), making the leading complexity as large as order d^(6α), before logarithms and unspecified constants. No calculation shows that the guarantees are non-vacuous at the experimental resolutions.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no code, and the manuscript omits exact augmentation ranges, selected image identifiers, masking and grayscale procedures, random seeds, epochs, batch sizes, stopping rules, and a complete specification of the empirical fully connected networks. The numerical results cannot be independently reconstructed from the paper.

Presentation is polished locally but not suitable for ICML as supplied: the main discussion occupies roughly 30 pages before extensive appendices, related work appears unusually late, and claims that the experiments “corroborate” the theory are overstated. The document is also author-identified and carries an arXiv identifier, which would violate anonymous-submission requirements if this were the actual review version. Overall, the theoretical idea has merit, but the technical gaps, narrow model, weak empirical validation, and poor reproducibility are important enough to prevent acceptance.

The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

strengths: Soundness: The paper precisely formulates a deformation-based generative model and gives explicit inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers. The upper-bound arguments in Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 provide useful insight into how pixel resolution creates O(1/d) approximation error under the stated smoothness and visibility assumptions.

Originality: Connecting deformation orbits, pixelization, matched-filter CNN representations, and statistical learning bounds is a nontrivial synthesis. The explicit CNN expressivity construction and separate analyses of 0-1 and clipped cross-entropy ERM are technically interesting.

Presentation and theoretical reproducibility: Assumptions, separation quantities, architectures, and theorem statements are mostly explicit, with extensive proofs and helpful illustrations in the complete manuscript and appendices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-geigt3gi/call-d2cac49534354469a3b9b20155902da3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly acknowledge the optimization-versus-ERM gap and difficulties involving background noise, clutter, multiple objects, occlusion, and sharp edges. The experiments use standard image datasets only as sources for synthetic templates, presenting low direct ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 3.8 does not establish the claimed optimality of the D≈1/d separation rate. It lower-bounds the ordinary distance ||f1-f0||/||f0||, whereas D in (12) and (23) is an infimum over brightness changes and deformations; a lower bound on the untransformed distance gives no lower bound on D. The construction also fixes the nuisance parameters before defining f1, so it directly proves ambiguity only for a chosen transformation or degenerate deformation law, not the asserted general random-deformation setting.

Soundness: The claimed applicability of Theorems 4.1–4.2 to non-invertible deformations is not supported by the proof. Proposition B.4, Proposition B.5, and equation (90) use support containment and change-of-variables properties that do not follow from Assumption 2(i) without global injectivity or additional boundary/truncation conditions.

The V/n result is a generic realizable-ERM upper bound, not an analysis of practical CNN training. The expressivity witness is effectively a bank of deformation-specific, full-image template filters, while all learning is delegated to ideal global ERM. The statement that V/n is minimax optimal cites a generic VC result but supplies no lower bound for this deformation model; indeed, the paper's own alignment classifiers obtain exact recovery once both classes are observed under related assumptions.

Significance is sharply limited by the data model: each class has one noiseless, nonnegative, smooth template; all within-class variation is generated by a common known deformation family; objects have zero background and remain fully visible; and labels are deterministic given the image. These assumptions exclude the intra-class semantic diversity, noise, texture, clutter, and partial visibility central to real image classification.

The experiments do not test ordinary MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-100, or ImageNet classification. They select one exemplar per class and generate every training and test image by deforming that same exemplar, using the same generator at test time. Consequently, near-zero error largely verifies the synthetic construction rather than supporting the manuscript's broader image-classification claims. The experiments also do not vary resolution or measure D, so neither the 1/d nor 1/sqrt(d) predictions are tested.

There is a major theory–experiment mismatch. The theory uses bounded parameters, structured potentially d×d filters, global max-pooling, a specific logarithmic-depth maximum network, clipped cross-entropy, and exact ERM. Table 1 instead reports 10×10 filters trained with Adam, without showing that these networks instantiate G(alpha,m), how width corresponds to |A_d^alpha|, or why the theoretical rate applies.

Empirical reproducibility is inadequate: no code is identified; transformation ranges and distributions, exemplar IDs, seeds, interpolation and background preprocessing, epoch count, batch size, stopping rule, and complete network topology are missing. Results use only 10 repetitions and 50 or 200 test samples, report medians without uncertainty, and include no standard-CNN, registration, equivariant-network, or scattering baseline.

Presentation contains consequential overstatements and correctable mathematical inconsistencies. For example, the L2 change of variables on page 50 uses xi·xi' instead of sqrt(xi·xi'), equation (37) has inconsistent test-set indexing, and phrases such as “corroborates the theoretical findings” and “minimax optimal” are stronger than the supplied evidence. Overall, the interesting theoretical direction does not overcome the unresolved central lower-bound claim, proof-scope gap, and weak validation.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript gives a precise deformation-based generative model and substantial, mostly self-contained proofs for the inverse-mapping, alignment, and CNN upper bounds (Theorems 3.1, 3.7, 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4). :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rs9oa315/call-a5686fd8823d4c01b99ab2fe078e0b62/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Originality and significance: Recasting image resolution as increasingly accurate observation of a deformed bivariate template—rather than increasing covariate dimension—is an insightful perspective. The explicit connection among functional alignment, deformation invariance, and CNN generalization is useful.

The CNN analysis is constructive: it explains how a bank of template/deformation filters and global max pooling can separate deformation orbits, then combines this with VC/entropy arguments for both 0-1 and cross-entropy ERM.

Presentation: The model, assumptions, classifiers, and main proof ideas are organized clearly, with effective figures and an unusually extensive appendix. The related-work discussion usefully connects functional data analysis, registration, scattering transforms, and equivariant networks.

The authors appropriately acknowledge major limitations, including background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, sharp edges, and the gap between ideal ERM and gradient-based training. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in this theoretical study using standard public benchmarks and synthetic transformations.
weaknesses: The claimed optimality of the D ≳ 1/d separation condition is not established. Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds only the ordinary normalized L2 distance between f0 and f1, whereas Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 use an infimum over brightness, scaling, translation, and deformation parameters. Because D can be smaller than the displayed L2 distance, the theorem does not provide the required lower bound on D.

Theorem 3.8 also has a material quantifier mismatch: its statement reads as though one pair f0,f1 works for every sufficiently large d, but the proof constructs f1 using the chosen d. As stated, equality of all increasingly fine pixel averages would force the templates to agree almost everywhere. The proof also writes an L2 change-of-variables factor as ξξ′ rather than sqrt(ξξ′); the intended rate appears repairable, but the theorem needs correction.

Significance is constrained by a very restrictive model: each class has one noiseless deterministic template, all intra-class variation is label-independent deformation and brightness, objects remain fully visible, and backgrounds are essentially zero. Consequently, the perfect-classification results with one example per class do not yet explain ordinary datasets containing pose, texture, instance, background, and label variation.

The evaluation is almost entirely model-conforming simulation: one selected image per class is deformed to create both training and test data. It neither evaluates natural within-class variability nor compares against standard CNN, augmentation, registration, equivariant-network, or nearest-neighbor baselines. It also does not vary the central theoretical quantities d and D or estimate the predicted rates, so the assertion that the experiments corroborate the theory is too strong.

Experimental reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript omits template identifiers, preprocessing/segmentation details, deformation ranges and distributions, seeds, epochs, batch sizes, stopping rules, and code. Equation (37) also treats N as the final sample index while later N denotes the test-set size, becoming inconsistent when training sets exceed N.

There is a substantial theory-practice gap beyond the honestly disclosed optimization issue. The theorems analyze ideal ERM over a specially structured, bounded-weight CNN determined by a deformation cover, while the experiments train differently specified Keras networks with Adam. Assumption 3 and the asserted cover cardinalities for the motivating deformation families are not formally verified, and no evidence connects the learned networks to the constructive filter-bank argument. These issues require significant revision before the central optimality and empirical claims can be relied upon.

strengths: Soundness/originality: The paper develops a precise deformation-orbit model of images and analyzes pixelization explicitly. Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 provide nontrivial resolution-dependent guarantees for inverse-mapping and alignment classifiers, supported by extensive proofs.

Significance: Modeling within-class randomness as geometric deformation rather than additive noise is an interesting statistical perspective. The link among functional-data alignment, template matching, invariant representations, and CNN generalization is potentially useful.

Methodology: The explicit CNN construction and the 0-1 and cross-entropy generalization bounds connect deformation-covering complexity, network size, image resolution, and sample size in a concrete way.

Presentation and limitations: The motivating figures and examples make the model intuitive, and the paper candidly identifies limitations involving background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, sharp edges, and optimization. The complete proof appendix aids theoretical reproducibility.
Ethics: The experiments use standard public image benchmarks only as sources for synthetic templates, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The CNN proofs appear to require an unstated support or injectivity condition. Assumption 2(i) gives supp(f) contained in A([0,1]^2), but Propositions B.4-B.5 repeatedly infer supp(f composed with A) contained in [0,1]^2 and use change-of-variables reasoning that does not follow for a general non-injective A. This directly conflicts with the claim that Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 do not require invertible deformations.

Soundness: Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds the ordinary normalized L2 distance between its constructed templates, not the orbit-based separation D used by the upper bounds. Without proving D is also of order 1/d, it does not establish the claimed optimality of the 1/d separation criterion as stated.

Evidence/significance: Every experimental class is generated by repeatedly deforming one selected image. Thus there is no natural within-class appearance variation, observation noise, clutter, occlusion, or realistic background, and the experiments largely reproduce the assumed generative model rather than validate it as a model of image classification.

Theory-experiment alignment: The theory uses ERM over specially constructed networks with full-image, block-structured filters indexed by a deformation cover. The experiments instead train conventional 10x10-filter CNNs with Adam, without identifying alpha, constructing the cover, or matching the theoretical architecture. Consequently, Figures 9-11 do not substantiate the stated rates or CNN mechanism.

Evaluation: There are no comparisons with ordinary nearest neighbors, augmentation, registration/template-matching systems, scattering transforms, or group-equivariant CNNs. Reporting only medians over 10 runs with 50 or 200 test examples and no dispersion further limits the conclusions.

Reproducibility: Crucial experimental details are absent, including deformation ranges and distributions, selected template IDs, splits and seeds, training epochs, batch size, stopping rule, complete layer specifications, preprocessing details, and code. The empirical results therefore cannot be reliably reproduced.

Presentation/reach: The 81-page manuscript is overly long for a main-track conference paper, while the practical scope remains narrow: exact zero background, a single template per class, known deformation families, fully visible objects, and ideal global ERM. The discussion acknowledges several of these limitations, but its claim of likely robustness to background noise via a CLT argument is speculative and unsupported.
